aspects.says: A volatile write on x86 costs a locked instruction or mfence to drain the write buffer.
aspects.reason: a claim about machine instructions and cost that no graded test can observe

aspects.says: Threads writing different variables on one cache line slow each other down, a performance effect rather than a correctness one.
The JIT may hoist a plain flag's read out of a loop so the loop never sees another thread's write, and volatile forbids that.
A reference can become visible before its object's fields are written, so a volatile reference or final fields are needed.
aspects.reason: practised on 5.1.1 by 'Publish an immutable polygon safely' and on 5.3.3 by 'Lazy initialization with double-checked locking'

aspects.says: The compiler, the JIT and the CPU may reorder a thread's operations as long as the thread's own view and every happens-before edge are kept.
basis: section:What the JMM Allows and Forbids

aspects.says: synchronized keeps the operations inside its block, but lets operations outside move in.
VarHandle's plain, opaque, release/acquire and volatile modes let code use only the ordering it needs.
aspects.reason: named as a Java feature; the weaker modes' ordering is not observable by a deterministic test

aspects.says: A volatile write keeps earlier accesses before it, and a volatile read keeps later accesses after it.
x86's strong ordering hides reorderings that ARM and POWER allow, so code must be correct by the JMM, not by one machine.

shortfalls.says: 2 of this quiz's 2 not-free readings are missing, negative or no longer about what they were taken over: the question 'Per this page, why can a JMM bug stay hidden in tests on x86 machines yet appear on ARM ones?' was judged and Q2 did not hold: from the question's text alone, the reader picked 'a'; the key is 'a', because the stem sets up a contrast between x86 and ARM; only option a uses a comparative wording ('fewer kinds'), fitting that contrast, while b and c state flat, absolute-sounding behaviors ('runs ... unoptimized', 'flushes ... when methods return') with no comparative link to ARM; the question 'Per this page, what is false sharing?' was judged and Q2 did not hold: from the question's text alone, the reader picked 'b'; the key is 'b', because the stem's term 'false sharing' decomposes into 'separate' (false, i.e. not truly the same variable) plus a shared resource (a cache line); option b names exactly that ('separate variables that live on one cache line'), while option a says 'one variable' (true, not false, sharing) and option c substitutes an unrelated word ('reorders') for any notion of sharing
